newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland needs fast growth to afford budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Poland needs fast growth to afford budget gap.

text.p: Poland's economy has to grow at least five to six percent annually to afford a budget deficit of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product as planned for 1997, an analyst from the independent CASE institute said.

Marek Dabrowski told journalists during a presentation of a report on fiscal policy in economies in transition that if the GDP growth rate fell to two-three percent or lower, a budget deficit of that size would be unsustainable.
"The size of the deficit at 2.8 percent is safe as long as the economy grows fast -- at five to six percent. But problems will start if it slows down," Dabrowski said.
"A different question is if fast growth can be maintained with a large budget deficit in the first place," he said.
The 1997 budget plan assumes a 5.5 percent real growth.

Dabrowski said Poland should not congratulate itself that its budget gap was below the three percent of GDP level set for European Union members because the country's economy was very different from those of EU members.

"Large countries with stable economies can sustain large budget gaps, but Poland's economy is neither large nor stable," he said. "Besides, Poland does not fulfil many other criteria, notably inflation, and they all work as a set."

Dabrowski said that of the two deficits which Poland runs -- the current account deficit seen at $6 billion this year and the budget deficit -- the fiscal one was a greater threat to the economy and should be tackled first.
"The budget deficit will fuel the growth of the current account deficit," Dabrowski said
"Even a large current account or trade gap does not have to be damaging to an economy when the budget is balanced, or better still, if there is a budget surplus," he said.
